items.title: Woolrich Europe elimina le pellicce animali dal 2027: la decisione dopo la campagna della Fur Free Alliance
items.description:
Woolrich Europe abbandona le pellicce animali dal 1° gennaio 2027 dopo la campagna della Fur Free Alliance con 200mila email e proteste nei negozi.
L'
items.body:
Moda

Woolrich Europe elimina le pellicce animali dal 2027: la decisione dopo la campagna della Fur Free Alliance

Roberto Torcolacci

-

24 Ottobre 2026

Dal 1° gennaio 2027, Woolrich Europe non produrrà più capi contenenti pellicce animali. L’annuncio, arrivato il 14 ottobre 2026, segna una svolta significativa per un marchio che ha fatto dell’outerwear di qualità la propria identità: la decisione di abbandonare le woolrich pellicce animali è il risultato diretto di una campagna internazionale coordinata dalla Fur Free Alliance, che ha mobilitato centinaia di migliaia di persone in tutta Europa con email, petizioni e proteste davanti ai negozi.
Una campagna che ha fatto la differenza
Dietro la scelta di Woolrich Europe c’è una pressione organizzata e prolungata. La Fur Free Alliance — rete internazionale che riunisce organizzazioni per la protezione degli animali attive in decine di paesi — ha condotto una campagna mirata contro l’uso delle pellicce nel marchio, ottenendo risultati concreti e misurabili.
Le azioni hanno incluso oltre 200.000 email inviate direttamente all’azienda e manifestazioni davanti ai punti vendita Woolrich in vari paesi europei. Non si è trattato di proteste sporadiche, ma di una strategia coordinata che ha combinato la pressione digitale con la visibilità fisica nei luoghi di acquisto, rendendo difficile ignorare il messaggio.
Questo tipo di campagna — che unisce l’attivismo online alla presenza sul territorio — si sta affermando come uno degli strumenti più efficaci per spingere i brand a rivedere le proprie politiche di approvvigionamento. Il caso Woolrich Europe ne è un esempio recente e documentato.Leggi ancheMade2Share: su Kickstarter la scarpa più sostenibile al mondoEcomoda: OVS, cotone 100% sostenibile entro il 2020
→ Leggi anche: Allevamenti intensivi di polpi e tonni, la Camera propone lo stop per proteggere il Mediterraneo
Cosa cambia concretamente dal 2027
A partire dal 1° gennaio 2027, Woolrich Europe cesserà la produzione di qualsiasi capo contenente pellicce di origine animale. Il marchio ha anche aderito al Fur Free Retailer Program, il programma internazionale che certifica i brand impegnati a eliminare le pellicce animali dalla propria offerta commerciale.
C’è però una distinzione importante da tenere presente: le collezioni già esistenti che contengono pellicce potranno continuare a essere vendute fino a esaurimento delle scorte. Questo significa che nei negozi Woolrich Europe potrebbero ancora essere presenti, per un periodo transitorio, articoli realizzati con materiali di origine animale. La discontinuità riguarda la produzione futura, non l’immediato ritiro dei prodotti già immessi sul mercato.
Si tratta di una pratica comune nelle transizioni di questo tipo, che consente ai brand di gestire le giacenze senza incorrere in perdite economiche eccessive, ma che può generare qualche ambiguità per i consumatori più attenti. Chi vuole acquistare capi certificati fur-free farebbe bene a verificare la data di produzione o a chiedere esplicitamente al personale di vendita.
Il contesto europeo sulle pellicce animali
La decisione di Woolrich Europe non arriva in un vuoto normativo. L’Unione Europea sta attraversando una fase di riflessione importante sul tema degli allevamenti da pelliccia: diversi paesi membri hanno già vietato o fortemente limitato questa pratica, e il dibattito a livello comunitario su una possibile regolamentazione più ampia è aperto.
L’annuncio di Woolrich Europe viene descritto esplicitamente come avvenuto «ahead of a crucial EU decision on fur farming» — in anticipo rispetto a una decisione cruciale dell’UE sugli allevamenti da pelliccia. Questo dettaglio non è secondario: posizionare la scelta aziendale prima di un eventuale obbligo normativo consente al marchio di presentarla come un atto volontario e proattivo, non come una risposta passiva a una legge già in vigore.
→ Leggi anche: Parlamento Europeo approva il divieto dei pallini di piombo nelle munizioni da caccia, tiro e pesca
Per i consumatori, questo contesto è utile per leggere l’annuncio nella sua dimensione strategica oltre che etica. I brand che anticipano le normative spesso lo fanno anche per motivi di posizionamento commerciale, oltre che per convinzione valoriale. Le due motivazioni non si escludono, ma è utile tenerle entrambe presenti.
Perché la questione woolrich pellicce animali riguarda anche i consumatori
Per chi acquista capi di abbigliamento tecnico e outdoor — il segmento in cui Woolrich opera storicamente — la provenienza dei materiali è diventata una variabile sempre più rilevante nelle decisioni d’acquisto. La pelliccia animale è stata a lungo utilizzata in questo settore per le sue proprietà termiche, ma negli ultimi anni le alternative sintetiche hanno raggiunto prestazioni comparabili, riducendo uno degli argomenti tecnici a favore del suo utilizzo.
Il fatto che un marchio come Woolrich Europe abbia risposto alla campagna della Fur Free Alliance con un impegno formale e datato — non con una dichiarazione vaga di intenti futuri — rappresenta un segnale di come stia cambiando il rapporto tra brand e comunità di consumatori consapevoli. Le 200.000 email inviate durante la campagna non sono un numero simbolico: indicano una base di persone disposte a dedicare tempo e attenzione a una singola questione legata a un singolo marchio.
Per chi vuole approfondire il tema delle pellicce nel settore moda e seguire l’evoluzione delle politiche aziendali, FOUR PAWS International ha pubblicato il comunicato ufficiale con i dettagli dell’annuncio e il contesto normativo europeo.
L’adesione al Fur Free Retailer Program implica anche un monitoraggio esterno della conformità agli impegni presi: non si tratta di una semplice dichiarazione, ma di un’iscrizione a un sistema di verifica riconosciuto a livello internazionale. Sarà questo il parametro con cui misurare, nei prossimi mesi e anni, se l’impegno annunciato il 14 ottobre 2026 si traduce in una trasformazione reale e duratura della filiera produttiva di Woolrich Europe.

items.title: Legge Gadda, dieci anni di lotta allo spreco alimentare: 10 miliardi di euro recuperati
items.description: La legge Gadda sullo spreco alimentare compie dieci anni: 10,3 miliardi di euro recuperati, 3,7 milioni di tonnellate di cibo e 40 milioni di farmaci
items.body:
Alimentazione

Legge Gadda, dieci anni di lotta allo spreco alimentare: 10 miliardi di euro recuperati

Roberto Torcolacci

-

24 Ottobre 2026

Dieci anni fa, l’Italia scelse un approccio radicalmente diverso al problema dello spreco alimentare: non sanzionare chi sprecava, ma rendere conveniente — e semplice — donare ciò che altrimenti sarebbe andato perduto. La legge Gadda sullo spreco alimentare, formalmente la Legge 166/2016, ha compiuto il suo primo decennio con un bilancio che supera ogni aspettativa iniziale: oltre 10,3 miliardi di euro di eccedenze alimentari e farmaceutiche recuperate e redistribuite, secondo la valutazione d’impatto condotta da Fondazione Terzjus ETS e Fondazione Valore con il supporto di Fondazione Cariplo, presentata alla Camera dei Deputati nell’ottobre 2026.
Un modello costruito sulla semplificazione, non sulla colpa
Prima del 2016, donare eccedenze alimentari in Italia era tecnicamente possibile ma burocraticamente complicato. Le imprese — dalla grande distribuzione ai produttori, dai ristoratori alle aziende agricole — si trovavano di fronte a una selva di adempimenti fiscali e amministrativi che rendeva la donazione meno conveniente dello smaltimento. Il risultato era paradossale: tonnellate di cibo perfettamente commestibile finivano in discarica mentre milioni di persone faticavano ad accedere a un’alimentazione adeguata.
La legge promossa da Maria Chiara Gadda, deputata che ne è rimasta la principale sostenitrice, ha ribaltato questa logica. Il principio cardine è la semplificazione: eliminare gli ostacoli normativi che scoraggiavano le donazioni, chiarire le responsabilità delle imprese donatrici, e costruire un canale diretto tra il mondo produttivo e il terzo settore. Niente sanzioni, niente burocrazia aggiuntiva — al contrario, meno adempimenti per chi sceglie di non sprecare.
Questo approccio ha dimostrato di funzionare proprio perché non chiede alle imprese uno sforzo straordinario, ma rimuove le barriere che rendevano lo sforzo ordinario troppo oneroso. Un’impresa che recupera e dona eccedenze non deve più temere contestazioni fiscali complesse o responsabilità sproporzionate per prodotti ancora integri ma prossimi alla scadenza.Leggi ancheOlio di sesamo per cucinare: 5 ricetteRicetta dell’Olio al basilico fatto in casa
I numeri del decennio: 3,7 milioni di tonnellate di cibo e 40 milioni di confezioni di farmaci
I dati raccolti nel rapporto d’impatto restituiscono la dimensione concreta di dieci anni di applicazione della norma. In totale, sono state recuperate 3,7 milioni di tonnellate di eccedenze alimentari: una quantità che, tradotta in termini quotidiani, equivale a sottrarre ogni giorno centinaia di camion di cibo dalla filiera dello smaltimento per redistribuirlo a chi ne ha bisogno.
Sul versante farmaceutico, il bilancio è altrettanto significativo: 40 milioni di confezioni di medicinali recuperate e rimesse in circolo attraverso il canale solidale. Si tratta di farmaci che, per ragioni di sovrapproduzione, cambio di formulazione o prossimità alla scadenza, sarebbero stati distrutti. Grazie alla legge, questi medicinali hanno raggiunto strutture del terzo settore, comunità in difficoltà, servizi di assistenza.
→ Leggi anche: Riciclo imballaggi in Italia: il 77,3% nel 2025 grazie al sistema Conai
Il valore complessivo stimato supera i 10,3 miliardi di euro: una cifra che non rappresenta solo un risparmio economico, ma la misura di una redistribuzione reale di risorse verso i segmenti più fragili della popolazione. L’evento celebrativo alla Camera dei Deputati ha offerto l’occasione per presentare questo bilancio e aprire una discussione su come la legge possa evolvere nei prossimi anni.
Come funziona concretamente il meccanismo di donazione
La Legge Gadda ha introdotto alcune semplificazioni operative che vale la pena comprendere per capire perché ha avuto successo. Prima di tutto, ha chiarito il regime fiscale delle donazioni: i beni ceduti gratuitamente a enti del terzo settore non vengono considerati autoconsumo ai fini IVA, eliminando così uno dei principali deterrenti per le imprese. Ha poi introdotto un sistema di comunicazione semplificato — in molti casi una sola comunicazione mensile invece di documentare ogni singola cessione — rendendo la gestione amministrativa compatibile con i ritmi operativi delle aziende.
Il modello prevede una rete di soggetti intermedi: food hub, banchi alimentari, organizzazioni di volontariato e strutture della Croce Rossa Italiana, che si occupano di raccogliere, stoccare e distribuire le eccedenze alle persone in stato di bisogno. Questo sistema a rete è fondamentale perché le imprese non devono gestire direttamente la distribuzione finale, ma semplicemente rendere disponibili le eccedenze a soggetti accreditati.
Non è un sistema perfetto — la logistica rimane una sfida, soprattutto per i prodotti freschi e deperibili che richiedono catene del freddo efficienti — ma ha dimostrato di essere scalabile e replicabile in contesti molto diversi tra loro, dalla grande distribuzione organizzata alle piccole realtà artigianali.
Il ruolo del terzo settore e la rete solidale italiana
Senza un terzo settore organizzato e capace, la legge sarebbe rimasta sulla carta. Una delle intuizioni più efficaci della normativa è stata proprio quella di valorizzare e strutturare il rapporto tra imprese e organizzazioni non profit, riconoscendo esplicitamente il ruolo di queste ultime come destinatari privilegiati delle eccedenze.
Organizzazioni come la Croce Rossa Italiana hanno sviluppato negli anni competenze specifiche nella gestione di questo tipo di flussi, costruendo infrastrutture logistiche dedicate e formando volontari in grado di operare secondo standard igienico-sanitari adeguati. Il risultato è una rete che oggi riesce a intercettare eccedenze in modo sistematico, non episodico.
→ Leggi anche: Allevamenti intensivi di polpi e tonni, la Camera propone lo stop per proteggere il Mediterraneo
Questo aspetto è spesso sottovalutato nel dibattito pubblico: il successo della Legge Gadda non è solo normativo, ma dipende dalla capacità del tessuto associativo italiano di trasformare le eccedenze in servizi concreti per le persone. I 10,3 miliardi di euro recuperati non sarebbero stati possibili senza questa infrastruttura umana e organizzativa.
Cosa resta da fare: i limiti di una legge che ha bisogno di evolvere
Un bilancio onesto non può ignorare i margini di miglioramento. Nonostante i risultati straordinari, lo spreco alimentare in Italia rimane un fenomeno rilevante: una parte significativa delle eccedenze prodotte lungo la filiera — in particolare nella fase agricola e nella ristorazione — non viene ancora intercettata dal sistema di recupero.
Le ragioni sono molteplici. Alcune riguardano la logistica: recuperare prodotti freschi da migliaia di piccoli produttori agricoli dispersi sul territorio è molto più complesso che gestire le eccedenze di un grande centro di distribuzione. Altre riguardano la consapevolezza: non tutte le imprese — soprattutto le più piccole — conoscono a fondo le opportunità offerte dalla legge e le procedure semplificate disponibili.
C’è poi la questione delle risorse destinate al terzo settore per sostenere questa funzione: la raccolta e redistribuzione di eccedenze ha un costo operativo reale, e la sostenibilità economica delle organizzazioni che svolgono questo ruolo non può essere data per scontata. Il dibattito aperto nell’ottobre 2026, a dieci anni dall’entrata in vigore della norma, ruota proprio attorno a questi nodi: come ampliare la platea dei donatori, come rafforzare la rete distributiva, come garantire continuità a un sistema che ha già dimostrato di valere miliardi.
Per approfondire il quadro normativo e i dati del rapporto d’impatto, il riferimento più aggiornato è il portale di Fondazione Terzjus ETS, che ha coordinato la valutazione decennale della legge.
Dieci anni non sono pochi, ma non sono nemmeno sufficienti per dichiarare chiuso un problema strutturale come lo spreco alimentare. Quello che la legge Gadda sullo spreco alimentare ha dimostrato è che un quadro normativo intelligente — che incentiva invece di sanzionare, che semplifica invece di complicare — può produrre risultati misurabili e duraturi. I 3,7 milioni di tonnellate di cibo e i 40 milioni di confezioni di farmaci recuperati in un decennio sono la prova che cambiare le regole del gioco, quando lo si fa con pragmatismo, funziona davvero.

Emulating absent land processes reduces carbon budgets in CMIP6 models
                        Spencer K. Liddicoat 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-5145-71531,2, Chris D. Jones 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-7141-92851,3, Lina M. Mercado

AbstractThe Transient Climate Response to cumulative Emissions (TCRE) is the cornerstone of estimates of carbon emissions budgets to future warming targets, characterising the near-linear relationship between the increase in global mean temperature and cumulative emissions of CO2. TCRE is derived from highly sophisticated Earth System Models (ESMs) - some, however, lack important processes known to have a large impact on TCRE. Here, we use multiple configurations of UKESM, a full-complexity ESM, to estimate how TCRE of 11 ESMs that participated in Coupled Model Intercomparison Project 6 would change if each included six terrestrial carbon cycle related processes present in UKESM, such as nitrogen limitation of photosynthesis and fire-vegetation interactions. We find that accounting for processes not included in the models increases their TCRE by an average of 21.4% implying a reduction of 16.0% ± 0.8% in the carbon budget for the transition from 1.5 °C to 2 °C.

Bay of Bengal cyclones fuel non-monsoon extreme precipitation on the central Tibetan Plateau
                        Gebanruo Chen1,2, Alexandre Cauquoin 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-4620-46963, Hans Christian Steen-Larsen

AbstractExtreme precipitation on the central Tibetan Plateau, particularly outside the summer monsoon season, strongly affects glacier mass balance and downstream water availability, yet the moisture transport mechanisms remain poorly understood. This study combines high-resolution measurements of the isotopic composition of atmospheric water vapour at Nam Co Lake with isotope-enabled climate model simulations to investigate an extreme snowfall event on 25 October 2022. We show that the event was triggered by a cyclonic disturbance over the northern Bay of Bengal, reinforced by the western Pacific subtropical high, which channelled moisture into the plateau interior. We identify a growing class of similar cyclone-driven extreme precipitation events before and after the monsoon season from 1990 to 2022. Climate projections indicate that such events will become more frequent under moderate and high emissions. These findings identify a robust isotopic fingerprint of cyclone–orography interactions and highlight the growing role of Bay of Bengal moisture in Tibetan Plateau water security in a warming climate.

items.title: In the synthetic biology era, engineered fungi could mitigate carbon dioxide emissions and enhance environmental resilience
items.body:
Download PDF

Review Article
    
        
            Open access

Published: 24 October 2026

In the synthetic biology era, engineered fungi could mitigate carbon dioxide emissions and enhance environmental resilience
                        Kyle Davis1 & Joanna Tannous 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-0032-51261

Communications Earth & Environment
                            volume 7,  Article number: 846 (2026) Cite this article
                        
                        
                            
    
        
            
                
                
                
                    
                    Save article
                
            
        
        
            
                View saved research

AbstractOver the past two decades, there has been a staggering increase in greenhouse gas emissions, particularly carbon dioxide (CO2) from unrestrained anthropogenic activities, leading to notable environmental shifts. Despite continuous efforts to reduce emissions, the world is not making satisfactory progress, which calls for immediate action to implement alternative strategies to enhance environmental sustainability. The Earth naturally absorbs and stores carbon through various processes, but merely keeping pace with ongoing human activities is no longer sufficient. Land plants and marine prokaryotes absorb CO2 during photosynthesis and store carbon as biomass. Eukaryotic organisms also represent a valuable resource that can provide insights into the biological fixation and removal of atmospheric CO2. Expanding the capacities of Earth’s natural systems offers enormous potential for enhancing carbon sinks and promoting environmental resilience. Although extensive synthetic engineering of plant systems has been conducted to enhance their native carbon fixation pathways, research on microorganisms, especially fungi, has been limited. In this review, we specifically explore the role of soil-borne fungi in carbon management, elucidating their responses to environmental shifts and their potential for climate change mitigation. We place particular emphasis on the role of various fungal guilds in this process, highlighting those that should be prioritized for future synthetic biology applications. We then engage with previous endeavors to address primary challenges in advancing genetic tools for these understudied fungi. Lastly, we discuss how integrating synthetic biology practices into the field of soil-associated fungi can drive advances in long-term carbon storage, enhance degradation of environmental pollutants, and improve nutrient exchange and soil health, contributing to more resilient soil ecosystems and sustainable environmental interventions. Rising carbon dioxide emissions from human activities are driving environmental change and increasing the need for strategies that strengthen natural carbon sinks and ecosystem resilience. While plants and microorganisms play important roles in carbon capture and storage, the potential of soil-associated fungi remains comparatively underexplored, particularly from a synthetic biology perspective. In this Review, we examine the roles of soil-borne fungi in carbon management, their responses to environmental change, and their potential contributions to climate change mitigation. We highlight key fungal guilds that could be prioritized for future synthetic biology applications and discuss current challenges in developing genetic tools for understudied fungi. Finally, we explore how engineering soil-associated fungi could support long-term carbon storage while providing broader environmental benefits, including pollutant degradation, nutrient exchange, and improved soil health. Together, these opportunities position fungal synthetic biology as a promising approach for developing more resilient soil ecosystems and sustainable environmental interventions.

IntroductionThe Industrial Revolution rapidly increased the emission of greenhouse gases (GHG) into the atmosphere, leading to radical changes in the global climatic pattern. Among GHGs, CO2 is the chief gas emitted and the prime contributor to global warming1. In May 2023, CO2 levels reached a new record of 424 ppm, recorded at Mauna Loa Observatory in Hawaii (https://www.climate.gov/), the highest in the modern record. While CO₂ concentrations were higher in Earth’s distant past, the current rise is unprecedented in speed. Projections estimate that atmospheric CO₂ could reach 540–970 ppm by 2100, depending on future emission trajectories. The shift toward renewable energy technology, such as electric vehicles and solar panels, has certainly reduced the further buildup of CO2 in the Earth’s atmosphere. However, addressing the climate challenge involves not only curbing new emissions but also dealing with the surplus of CO2 already present in the atmosphere. Terrestrial ecosystems have been acknowledged as the main sinks for global CO2 emissions. Forest trees are crucial in carbon removal and storage, as they sequester CO2 and convert it into plant biomass through photosynthesis2,3. In recent years, the concept of sustainable biological carbon sequestration has attracted attention from the research community. Indeed, the field has recently seen an incredible amount of research aiming to enhance various plant systems’ carbon sequestration abilities, either through the engineering of crops with stronger and deeper root systems to promote carbon flow below ground4 or by modifying the metabolism of plant cells to improve photosynthesis5,6. Bioengineering of soils has also emerged as a promising approach to enhance carbon sequestration7.Besides living trees, rhizosphere-resident fungi are the key drivers of nutrient cycling and biological carbon fixation across global ecosystems as a result of their interactions with growing and decaying vegetation and their associated microbiomes8. Studies have shown that soil-borne fungi contribute ~20% more to carbon storage in agricultural soils than do bacteria9. This advantage is partly due to their greater resilience in a wide range of soil conditions, including acidic, nutrient-poor, and drought-affected environments, conditions in which bacterial populations often decline10,11. Fungal hyphae can also form persistent networks that stabilize soil aggregates and physically protect organic matter, further enhancing carbon retention12. Additionally, fungi tend to have slower biomass turnover and higher carbon use efficiency than bacteria, allowing more carbon to be stored as biomass rather than lost as CO₂ through respiration13. In contrast, bacteria typically dominate the early stages of decomposition, rapidly processing simple organic compounds but contributing less to long-term carbon stabilization due to their faster turnover and lower capacity to handle complex substrates like lignin and cellulose. These soil-associated fungi can be categorized into various guilds based on their ecological roles and interactions with their host. Saprotrophic fungi, for example, such as many yeasts and molds, decompose dead organic matter, recycling nutrients back into the soil and influencing carbon dynamics. In contrast, biotrophs obtain nutrients from living host organisms without causing immediate harm, maintaining a balanced relationship to ensure their own survival. Lastly, obligate biotrophs, a subset of biotrophs, rely entirely on living hosts for their nutrition and cannot survive or reproduce without them. Examples include arbuscular mycorrhiza (AM) fungi, which form symbiotic relationships with plant roots to enhance nutrient uptake, and are hosted by ~70% of all terrestrial plant species14,15. In the era of synthetic biology, comprehending the roles of various fungal guilds is crucial for developing bioengineering strategies to enhance soil carbon sequestration, thereby combating climate change. However, these organisms have been largely overlooked as powerful allies in this endeavor. One of the primary challenges in leveraging the potential of soil fungi to influence carbon cycling lies in our limited understanding of the complex soil ecosystems they inhabit and the molecular mechanisms through which they interact with plants to affect CO₂ sequestration. Thus, enhancing the identification and functional characterization of these soil fungal communities will improve predictions of their roles and responses to global environmental changes. This understanding will also facilitate efforts to manage and utilize fungal species to support plant carbon fixation and reduce greenhouse gas emissions.As our understanding of the role of soil fungi in the global carbon cycle continues to evolve, it is increasingly clear that they are more important than previously thought. This review aims to untangle the complex relationship between fungi and global warming while highlighting the direct and indirect contributions of various fungal guilds to the biological fixation of carbon in soil. Additionally, this review focuses on the progress made in genetically engineering these fungal groups and the potential avenues to enhance the capabilities of fungal synthetic biology across a range of applications—through engineering synthetic symbiosis, synthetic autotrophy, or synthetic CO2-assimilation pathways. This knowledge is crucial for establishing systematic microbial management strategies to mitigate planet-warming GHGs from a fungal perspective.Fungi and global warming: “all give no take” relationshipFungal carbon dynamics: key drivers of soil carbon storageSoil microbes play a crucial role in the global warming dilemma by controlling the turnover of soil organic matter, the largest organic carbon pool in the terrestrial biosphere16, which stores ~1500 GtC in the top meter and up to ~2400 GtC in the upper two meters of global soils17. However, the soil microbial community, often regarded as a “black box”18, is complex and not fully understood. Within this “black box,” fungi, including free-living and plant-associated species, are considered particularly important for storing carbon in the soil. Among others, mycorrhizal fungi have been identified as essential players in soil carbon pools because they form a vast subterranean hyphal network using carbon as their building block. A recent study estimated that ~3.58 Gt C y⁻¹ fixed by terrestrial plants is directed to their mycorrhizal partners underground19, representing a substantial fraction of photosynthetically fixed carbon. This is particularly striking when considering the distribution of biomass across all taxa on Earth; plants dominate with 450 Gt C, bacteria contribute 70 Gt C, and fungi account for 12 Gt C, underscoring the significant role of fungi in the global carbon cycle20. For context, the 2024 State of Carbon Dioxide Removal report, co-led by University of Oxford researchers, estimates that achieving climate targets will require the removal of approximately 1.9–2.4 Gt C y⁻¹ from the atmosphere by mid-century21, placing mycorrhizal carbon fluxes on a comparable order of magnitude. While forming their “web-like” patterns in the soil, mycorrhizal fungi develop specialized symbiotic interfaces with their host plant for nutrient and carbon exchange22,23. Crucially, this symbiosis is functionally diverse, with arbuscular mycorrhiza (AM) and ectomycorrhiza (EcM), the two most widespread and well-studied types24, differing in how they influence carbon allocation and storage. Terrestrial plants allocate roughly 1.07 Gt C yr⁻¹ to AM fungi and ~2.47 Gt C yr⁻¹ to EcM fungi, together accounting for approximately 36% of current annual fossil-fuel CO₂ emissions19. These guilds differ in their effects on carbon storage pathways: AM fungi primarily influence carbon retention in living plant biomass, whereas EcM fungi more directly enhance soil carbon storage25. In EcM-dominated systems, soil carbon stocks can be up to ~70% higher than in AM-dominated systems, likely due to more efficient nitrogen acquisition that suppresses microbial decomposition and promotes organic matter accumulation26. Field experiments further show that EcM fungi can reduce soil organic carbon respiration by as much as 67%27, while AM fungi produce more modest increases in soil organic carbon (averaging ~21.5% in controlled studies), with context-dependent effects in natural ecosystems28. These root symbionts have been found to help store carbon in the soil through different processes, including channeling plant-derived carbon into recalcitrant biomass, stabilizing organic matter within soil aggregates, and suppressing decomposition through nutrient competition. In this regard, it has been reported that the competition for nitrogen between symbiotic EcM fungi and free-living microbial decomposers can decrease soil carbon respiration, ultimately resulting in higher soil carbon storage in ectomycorrhizal ecosystems globally27. For many years, AM fungi were believed to enhance nutrient storage and protect soil C from degradation by improving soil structure through the production of the glycoprotein glomalin or glomalin-related soil proteins (GRSP)29. These proteins were reported to contribute directly to stabilizing soil organic matter following hyphal death by acting as a biological glue that binds soil particles to form aggregates that protect stored soil carbon from escaping30. However, recent research has prompted a reevaluation of GRSP’s properties and their exact role in soil ecosystems. Holátko et al. suggest that what has been traditionally identified as glomalin or GRSP may, in fact, be a complex mixture of heat-stable proteins, humic substances, and other soil organic matter components31. This complexity challenges previous assumptions about GRSP’s origin, composition, and function, raising several fundamental questions for future research. In this context, soil aggregation by these symbionts is also linked to specific root and mycorrhizal fungal traits, including hyphal length and density, branching and entangling capacity, tensile strength, and the production of extracellular compounds32,33. These traits influence aggregate formation and stabilization, which in turn regulate carbon incorporation and persistence within aggregates and its distribution between labile and more stable, mineral-associated pools33. Along these lines, studies have also shown that greater soil biotic and fungal diversity can positively influence aggregate stability by supporting a wider range of biological interactions and aggregation mechanisms operating within the soil matrix. Moreover, functional traits such as motility, body size, and population density can further enhance aggregate stability and persistence34. In addition to their substantial contribution to the soil organic carbon pool as living fungal biomass, these biotrophic symbionts leave a legacy after they die, as their hyphae contribute to necromass that can be biochemically stabilized (e.g., chitin-rich residues) and incorporated into longer-lived soil organic matter, particularly in systems with low disturbance35. The persistence of fungal-derived C varies considerably depending on fungal traits, environmental conditions, and stabilization mechanisms. While living mycorrhizal mycelium can turn over on timescales of weeks36, fungal residues can persist considerably longer. For example, a three-year field decomposition experiment found that up to ~20% of fungal necromass remained at the end of the study, with persistence varying considerably depending on necromass properties. Although the experiment was not exclusively focused on mycorrhizal fungi, these findings provide evidence that a fraction of fungal-derived C can persist in soils over multi-year timescales37. Persistence can extend further when microbial-derived residues become associated with soil minerals, with estimated mean residence times of mineral-associated microbial necromass C on the order of decades (~24–67 years), although these estimates are not specific to fungi and vary among soils and environmental conditions38. In this regard, melanin has been shown to mitigate the accelerated decay of mycorrhizal necromass, thereby increasing long-term storage of carbon in soil organic matter39. Lastly, another important mechanism by which mycorrhizal fungi contribute to carbon sequestration is through the enhancement of mineral weathering and dissolution. In symbiosis with plant roots, EcM fungi extend hyphal networks into the soil that colonize mineral surfaces and release organic acids and protons that accelerate mineral breakdown. This weathering mobilizes nutrients such as calcium, magnesium, and phosphorus that support plant growth and sustain the fungal–plant association40,41,42. The released cations can react with dissolved inorganic carbon derived from atmospheric CO₂ to form carbonate minerals, such as calcium carbonate (CaCO₃), under favorable geochemical conditions, contributing to long-term carbon sequestration43. However, carbonate precipitation in soils is strongly influenced by soil type, pH, hydrology, and seasonal rainfall patterns. Previous studies have shown that CaCO₃ may periodically dissolve and re-precipitate depending on soil texture and mineral feedstock, making long-term stabilization difficult to assess44. Moreover, excessive carbonate accumulation may increase soil alkalinity and reduce the availability of micronutrients, potentially limiting the growth of plant species that are not adapted to high-pH soils45.In addition to mycorrhizal fungi, other soil fungal guilds have been positioned as a critical entry point of carbon into soil systems. In this regard, endophytic fungi that establish mutualistic associations with diverse plant species, thereby boosting their endogenous tolerance mechanism against various stresses, were also shown to be critical contributors to soil carbon sequestration because of their role in increasing plant biomass yield and improving photosynthesis46. Similar to mycorrhizal fungi, certain endophytic fungi were also reported to play a significant role in soil carbon sequestration through mineral weathering. For example, urease-positive fungi isolated from calcareous soils have been demonstrated to induce CaCO₃ precipitation, highlighting the role of these soil fungi in microbially mediated carbonate formation47. However, the enhancement of urease activity in soil also has important agronomic and environmental implications. A substantial body of literature has documented that elevated urease activity accelerates the hydrolysis of urea fertilizers, leading to increased emissions of ammonia (NH₃), reduced nitrogen use efficiency, and potential environmental pollution48,49. Therefore, while urease-producing fungi may contribute to carbonate precipitation and carbon sequestration, their broader impacts on nitrogen cycling and gaseous nitrogen losses must be carefully considered in agricultural systems. Alongside mineral weathering, fungal nitrate assimilation may also promote CO₂ mineralization through biologically driven alkalinization and associated carbonate precipitation. For example, it has been demonstrated that Alternaria species can induce CaCO₃ precipitation in agar-based microcosms supplied with calcium nitrate, suggesting that fungal nitrate assimilation can contribute to inorganic carbon sequestration under controlled conditions50. While the study did not examine soil systems directly, it highlights the broader potential for fungal nitrogen metabolism to influence coupled carbon and nitrogen biogeochemical processes50. Furthermore, some soil yeasts broadly defined as unicellular fungi have been reported to enhance various soil parameters, including organic carbon storage51. Numerous soil yeast species have also been found to possess plant growth-promoting abilities by producing indole-3-acetic acid (IAA), siderophores, and extracellular enzymes52. As mentioned above, soils constitute the largest terrestrial organic carbon pool, making them an important target for climate change mitigation through enhanced carbon sequestration. In this regard, restorative land management practices, including conservation tillage, cover cropping, crop residue retention, and organic amendments, have been estimated to sequester ~0.9 ± 0.3 Gt C yr⁻¹ globally53. However, their long-term sequestration potential is limited by saturation as soil approaches a new equilibrium, the risk of reversal under changing land management or climatic conditions, and trade-offs with agricultural productivity and food security objectives54. Likewise, afforestation and reforestation have been identified as major nature-based CDR strategies, with the IPCC (2019) estimating a global CO₂ removal potential ranging from ~0.14–2.73 Gt C yr⁻¹ during the 2020–2050 period, depending on land availability, governance, biodiversity safeguards, and food-system tradeoffs55. Along the same line, global biochar deployment has been estimated to avoid up to ~1–1.8 Gt C yr⁻¹ of emissions, depending on feedstock availability, land-use constraints, and accounting assumptions56. Similarly, enhanced rock weathering (ERW) accelerates natural silicate weathering through the application of finely crushed silicate rocks to soils, where plant–microbe-soil interactions can further enhance mineral dissolution and CO₂ uptake. Approximately ~3.58 Gt C yr⁻¹ is transferred annually from plants to mycorrhizal networks, highlighting the substantial scale at which fungi participate in terrestrial carbon cycling. These observations suggest that fungal processes may represent an underexplored component of climate change mitigation, with the potential to influence the effectiveness and long-term stability of carbon sequestration across existing land-based CDR strategies.Global warming drastically impacts fungal attributesThe current literature not only highlights the significance of soil fungi in mitigating the greenhouse effect, but it also offers valuable insights into how these fungi respond to the consequences of ongoing global changes. Beyond altering community composition and diversity, shifting climate patterns influence fungal physiology, such as fruiting times, growth rates, sporulation, and metabolism, including the production of specialized metabolites and mycotoxins. These environmental changes also affect the nature and outcomes of fungal symbioses with plants, sometimes reducing mutualistic benefits and altering nutrient exchange dynamics. In addition, rising temperatures, altered precipitation, and extreme weather events are driving the emergence and spread of fungal pathogens that threaten humans, animals, and plants. Altogether, these impacts highlight the need to understand and anticipate how climate-driven shifts in fungal traits and interactions will cascade through ecosystems and affect global food security, biodiversity, and public health.Impacts on fungal communities and diversityClimate change is causing a worldwide shift in the distribution of plants57, challenging certain species and putting their communities and diversity at risk of significant losses58. The same climate factors impacting plant communities are expected to significantly affect their associated fungal communities. The influence varies based on the ecological guild: filamentous fungi, including EcM, thrive at higher temperatures, whereas yeasts decrease59. Research on forest disturbances, like fires and pest outbreaks, reveals that the composition of soil fungi after such events is determined by both the fungal guild and the nature of the disturbance. These occurrences can lead to a significant shift from predominantly EcM fungi to saprotrophic fungi60,61. Recently, the effects of climate change on the community composition and diversity of soil fungi have been comprehensively reviewed62. The authors stress the need for continuous monitoring and data acquisition to effectively model different environments across the globe.Impacts on fungal physiologyResearch studying global warming’s physiological impact on fungi has primarily focused on fruiting time and sporulation as indicators of mycelial activity. The fruiting times of diverse fungi have already shifted in response to rising temperatures. The extent to which a specific species is influenced, however, depends on abiotic factors such as temperature, precipitation, light, soil moisture, and nutrient availability63. Fruiting in cooler biomes is particularly sensitive to temperature increases, leading to earlier and prolonged fruiting periods63,64. Warming temperatures have led to earlier spring fruiting and delayed autumnal fruiting in several EcM fungal species65. Similarly, the sporulation of plant pathogenic ascomycetes has also shifted to earlier timing and longer durations66,67,68. This timing shift, together with increased precipitation, also affected the spores’ size. Research has shown that spores released in early autumn tend to be larger than those released in late autumn due to increased water accumulation69. The growth rates of fungi were also affected by climate change, with the growth of certain mycotoxigenic fungi having been enhanced by elevated temperatures70. Overall, the impact of climate change on fungal fruiting, growth, and sporulation can have significant consequences on fungal symbioses, invasion, and pathogenesis. More extensive studies on different components of fungal physiology are required to elucidate the full effects of elevated temperatures, CO2 levels, and precipitation on fungi and their interactions with ecosystems.Impacts on fungal metabolismClimate is the main impetus of fungal colonization and specialized metabolite and mycotoxin biosynthesis71. Therefore, fluctuations in atmospheric CO2 levels, environmental temperature, and precipitation could result in startling changes in mycotoxin contamination of crops in the field and post-harvest. In this regard, it was found that the production of aflatoxin B1 by Aspergillus flavus, an opportunistic pathogen of oilseed crops, was significantly influenced by a combination of these environmental factors72,73. Similar studies in Fusarium species have found that water availability and temperature largely influence the production of fumonisins, trichothecenes, and deoxynivalenol74,75,76,77,78. Similarly, a review on Aspergillus, Penicillium, and Fusarium species reports that climate change-driven temperature increases and altered water availability enhance mycotoxin production in these species, threatening global crops77. To mitigate these impacts, a framework combining predictive climate modeling, adaptive agricultural practices, and CO2 emission reductions has been proposed78.Impacts on fungal symbiosis with plantsIncreased CO2 and temperatures reduce plant growth due to symbiont competition driven by resource allocation79. EcM fungi showed diverse responses to elevated CO2 levels, with some species exhibiting altered biomass production and respiration80. Similarly, elevated temperatures and limited water availability significantly altered the EcM community composition, favoring species with restricted mycelial growth and shorter turnover times81. These studies suggest that climate change could intensify competition in favor of EcM species that thrive in these conditions, potentially impacting plant hosts negatively.Research on the impact of climate change on AM fungal species and their plant symbionts has revealed conflicting results82. Under higher temperatures and reduced rainfall, root biomass, AM colonization, abundance, and diversity were found to be negatively affected83,84,85. Under similar conditions, researchers have also documented a shift from AM fungal species that primarily allocate biomass to produce external hyphae to those that allocate biomass for root colonization and root–root linkage86. A more recent study found that higher temperatures and increased CO2 levels led to a greater diversity of AM fungi in maize and wheat; in contrast with previous studies, root colonization of these plants decreased under these conditions87.Other plant endosymbionts are also affected by climate change. Elevated CO2 increased colonization of Epichloë coenophiala (Neotyphodium coenophialum) in Lolium arundinaceum88. A shift in the dynamics of the fungus Beauveria bassiana and its host plant, Zea mays, from mutualism to commensalism was reported under increased temperatures89. A recent study reported that the species Metarhizium robertsii increased root colonization and plant height in Zea mays under drought conditions90.Impacts on fungal infectionsIncreased temperatures, droughts, flooding, and natural disasters driven by global warming have influenced the emergence of fungal pathogens91. Increased temperatures have selected for thermotolerant fungal strains that can grow in conditions that are historically unfavorable for growth92. A directed evolution experiment in the entomopathogenic fungus Metarhizium anisopliae demonstrated that this fungus can be adapted from its normal upper limit of 32 °C to grow at 37 °C while retaining its pathogenicity93. A previous review summarized examples of fungal outbreaks following natural disasters, including earthquakes, tsunamis, hurricanes, volcanic eruptions, and dust storms94. Together, these factors raise concerns about the emergence of new pathogens that can infect humans, animals, and plants as climate change worsens.One hypothesis for the simultaneous emergence of the human pathogen Candida auris across multiple global regions posits elevated global temperatures as a potential driver95,96, though this emergence has also been hypothesized to have resulted from other factors, including fungicide contamination in the environment and transmission within and across healthcare systems96,97. Cryptococcus species, known for causing cryptococcosis, are among the biggest fungal threats in a healthcare environment for immunocompromised individuals. White-nose syndrome in bats, caused by Pseudogymnoascus destructans, is another recently emerged fungal disease that primarily affects hibernating bats and is expected to drive several species to extinction101. As the climate warms, so does the temperature at which bats hibernate. A previous study found that bats subjected to warmer hibernation temperatures developed higher fungal loads and suffered greater impacts from the disease102. The spread of the chytridiomycete fungus Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis, which has decimated amphibian populations around the world, has been associated with temperature and humidity variability resulting from climate change103,104. Rising temperatures select for heat-tolerant strains, enabling fungi like Candida auris to infect humans, and Cryptococcus deuterogattii to expand into temperate regions. Extreme weather events further facilitate fungal dispersal, leading to outbreaks following natural disasters. In wildlife, warmer conditions exacerbate diseases such as white-nose syndrome in bats and chytridiomycosis in amphibians. Agricultural systems are also at risk, with thermotolerant plant pathogens like Puccinia striiformis and Fusarium graminearum spreading to new regions, threatening food security.Current available tools for the genetic manipulation of soil-borne fungiBuilding upon our previous discussion of the diverse fungal guilds and types and their known mechanisms through which they contribute to carbon cycling and sequestration, we now delve into the genetic tools available for transforming these organisms. Understanding and leveraging these methodologies are vital for enhancing the innate capabilities of soil-associated fungi, paving the way for targeted engineering strategies to amplify their role in carbon sequestration and address critical climate challenges.Current methods for transforming fungi include biolistic bombardment, electroporation-mediated transformation, polyethylene glycol (PEG)–mediated protoplast transformation, and Agrobacterium-mediated transformation (AMT)110. Traditionally, most of these methods have relied on linearized plasmid integration with very little targeting efficiency in filamentous fungi due to their propensity to repair DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) using non-homologous end joining (NHEJ)111. This has typically resulted in the insertion of donor DNA into random genomic loci even when flanking sequences designed for homology-directed repair (HDR) are used112. In contrast, yeasts predominantly repair DSBs through HDR113. Recent advancements utilizing technologies such as the bacterial defense-based Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeat (CRISPR)–CRISPR-associated protein 9 (Cas9) system in filamentous fungi have allowed for much higher transformation efficiencies and specificity114. Engineering model fungal species has enabled significant advancements in large-scale biomanufacturing. However, limited documentation exists on engineering soil-borne fungi due to the challenges of working with these species and the lack of available sequenced genomes. A summary of the available genetic tools for these fungi and their applications is provided in this section. It is important to note that most of these tools have not yet been directly applied to carbon sequestration strategies; rather, many of the highlighted studies serve as proof-of-concept demonstrations for genetic manipulation in these organisms. Nevertheless, these emerging tools provide a foundation for future targeted functional studies aligned with the carbon management and sequestration strategies proposed in Section 4.Genetic tools for EcM fungiGenetic tools available for EcM fungi are limited; some examples are listed in Table 2. Overall, introducing genetic elements is non-targeted and relies on random integration into the genome. Only for a few species of EcM have protoplasts been harvested and regenerated successfully for transformation115,116. However, these methods cannot control the number of copies integrated into the recipient genome. One advantage of this method is the ability to co-transform separate plasmids into the same recipient, as demonstrated previously in Hebeloma cylindrosporum117. Biolistic, or particle, bombardment is a technology used to introduce genetic material into fungi without the need to protoplast them. This technique has been successfully used to introduce green fluorescent protein (gfp) and hygromycin resistance (hph) genes into Pisolithus tinctorius118. AMT also bypasses the need to protoplast by enabling direct transformation of fungal mycelium or conidia through co-cultivation with Agrobacterium tumefaciens carrying the desired constructs119. This technique has been shown to be effective in introducing knockout constructs and RNA interference (RNAi) constructs, facilitating targeted gene disruption and gene silencing in various EcM fungal species, including Hebeloma cylindrosporum, Suillus bovinus, Paxillus involutus120, Laccaria bicolor121, Tuber borchii122, and Laccaria laccata123. To date, the CRISPR-Cas9 system has not been applied to EcM fungi. Transformation of these fungi has been facilitated using biolistic technology to introduce foreign DNA combined with selectable markers. This approach has been used successfully with Gigaspora rosea125 and Glomus intraradices126 to introduce β-glucuronidase and fluorescent reporters, respectively. Agrobacterium-mediated transformation was also employed in G. intraradices, but the efficiency was very low126. Various yeasts, including soil-borne species, have been genetically engineered exclusively for biotechnological and industrial applications. The electroporation-based gene delivery approach has been extensively employed in yeast transformation for decades, with protocols established in various soil-associated species, including Candida tropicalis142, Wickerhamomyces anomalus143, and Pichia pastoris (syn. Komagataella spp)144. These protocols involve the use of lithium acetate or heat shock to enhance transformation efficiency. PEG-mediated protoplast transformation and AMT have also been widely used in yeast species from soil such as Lipomyces starkeyi147, Cryptococcus sp.148, and Rhodotorula mucilaginosa149. More recently, CRISPR-Cas9–mediated genome editing via protoplast-based transformation has also been established in some species, such as Aureobasidium pullulans150. In recent years, the development of genome-wide CRISPR-based libraries in model yeast species, such as Saccharomyces cerevisiae, has significantly advanced functional genomics151,152. These developments in S. cerevisiae hold promise for applying these tools to non-conventional yeast species, including those associated with soil and rhizosphere environments, which often present unique biological and ecological insights deserving of further exploration through synthetic biology approaches. Lastly, adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE) has been used to harness natural selection for developing yeast strains with enhanced or novel phenotypes. While it doesn’t involve direct genetic manipulation like CRISPR or traditional genetic engineering techniques, ALE is considered a genetic tool because it induces genetic changes through controlled environmental pressures, making it a valuable tool in strain development. To name a few examples, in the thermotolerant yeast Pichia kudriavzevii, isolated from soil, ALE under acetic acid stress has enhanced multistress tolerance, improving the strain's suitability for industrial applications153. Similarly, in Candida tropicalis, a xylose-fermenting yeast, ALE has been used to improve thermotolerance and glucose tolerance, enhancing its potential for bioethanol production154.Unlocking the potential of fungal synthetic biology to tackle atmospheric greenhouse gas emissionsAlthough progress has been made toward genetically manipulating fungi from the various guilds explored above, the potential for engineering these species to reduce the impact of anthropogenic climate change has yet to be explored. Avenues for engineering plants and bacteria to enhance agricultural productivity and increase CO2 sequestration, with a brief mention of mycorrhizal fungi, have been proposed previously155. Some suggested approaches include altering biomass accumulation and plant architecture through boosting phytohormone production156, boosting plant defenses and stress tolerance through altering secondary metabolite production157, introducing and improving nitrogen fixation pathways into fungi158, boosting atmospheric CO2 drawdown159, and engineering pathways for producing useful materials and/or degradation of waste products such as plastics160. Similar synthetic biology applications could also be explored for implementation in soil-borne fungi to enhance their ability to capture, sequester, and store carbon that would otherwise remain in the atmosphere. While methods developed for bacteria and plants provide a valuable foundation, investing time and research into fungi-specific engineering is critical due to their unique advantages. Fungi are inherently more resilient in harsh environments, such as extreme temperatures, acidic or saline soils, and nutrient-poor ecosystems, where plants and bacteria might struggle to survive. Additionally, their vast mycelial networks can span large areas, enabling efficient carbon capture and nutrient cycling at a scale unattainable by individual bacteria or plant roots. In previous sections, we examined how different fungal guilds contribute directly or indirectly to the long-term storage of carbon and discussed the current genome editing tools available for these fungi. This knowledge offers a biological framework for applying fungal synthetic biology to genetically enhance these desirable traits beyond their natural capabilities or introduce them in fungal lineages that lack them naturally. Below, we summarize some potential strategies that can be implemented to engineer and reconfigure traits in fungi to help address GHG emissions and the climate change dilemma (Fig. 1). Despite the promise of engineered fungi in mitigating GHG emissions, efforts to date often neglect critical biosafety risks, regulatory oversight, and broader societal acceptance. Deploying genetically engineered microbes, including fungi, in environmental settings raises legitimate concerns regarding ecological disruption, horizontal gene transfer, and unintended persistence. Their field deployment may also face regulatory and societal barriers, particularly in regions with strong opposition to genetically modified organisms. For example, EU Regulation 2019/1009 recognizes mycorrhizal fungi as microbial biostimulants, but limitations in the classification and scope of permitted microorganisms may constrain the application of emerging microbial technologies161. Moreover, standardized approaches for evaluating the efficacy of biocontainment strategies under complex, real-world environmental conditions remain limited162. Addressing these challenges will require clear, case-specific risk assessment and regulatory pathways, together with transparent communication and public engagement. To address biosafety concerns, researchers are advancing intrinsic biocontainment strategies, such as synthetic auxotrophy and programmable kill switches, designed to restrict microbe viability outside controlled settings163,164. Integrating these safeguards into fungal engineering pipelines is essential not only for environmental protection but also for building public trust and aligning innovation with regulatory and societal expectations. However, technical safeguards alone may not ensure societal acceptance. Transparent communication of potential benefits and risks, stakeholder engagement early in technology development, and accessible monitoring and risk-assessment frameworks will be important for building public trust, particularly in regions where genetically modified organisms face substantial public opposition.Fig. 1: Conceptual overview of fungal engineering strategies to improve carbon sequestration and plant growth through optimized synthetic biology approaches.Full size imageThese approaches include development of synthetic symbiosis, synthetic CO2-assimilating and bioremediation pathways, and synthetic enhancement of key fungal traits such as GRSP and melanin biosynthesis. Integrating these approaches will improve plant growth and disease resistance, promote biomass production, enhance long-term carbon storage, and reduce greenhouse gas emissions, contributing to environmental sustainability.Engineering fungal traits to enhance fungal–plant symbiosesSymbiotic association between plants and fungi is a fundamental driver of plant growth and development, as fungi enhance nutrient and water uptake, particularly phosphorus and nitrogen, in exchange for plant-derived carbohydrates. This improved nutrient acquisition supports greater photosynthetic capacity and root biomass, which in turn increases the amount of atmospheric CO₂ fixed into plant tissues and stored in soils, thereby enhancing carbon sequestration. Therefore, one potential application of synthetic biology in soil-borne fungi is to engineer strains capable of promoting plant health and growth through mutualistic symbioses. This can be achieved by enhancing the production of specific endophytic fungal metabolites that are known to play crucial roles in plant–fungal symbiosis. These metabolites include terpenoids, phytohormones, siderophores, vitamins, antibiotics, organic acids, lytic enzymes, and volatile organic compounds165,166. Recently, a restricted set of carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZymes) has been exclusively reported in some lineages of mycorrhizal fungi (orchid [OrM] and ericoid [ErM] mycorrhizal fungi). The nod genes responsible for LCO production are well characterized in soil rhizobial bacteria169, and orthologs have been identified in fungi, but their functions have not yet been validated168. Efforts have been directed toward engineering Nod factor receptors in crops to activate symbiosis pathways170. To our knowledge, no engineering work has been undertaken on the microbe side, although it is firmly established that the induction of Nod factor biosynthesis is controlled by two copies of the nodD gene in Rhizobium171. Great effort has been put into engineering nitrogen fixation directly into plants, but this process has yet to be successfully implemented173,174,175. AM and EcM fungi could also be considered as platforms for engineering nitrogen fixation themselves, though such an approach presents many challenges—including the expression of a large set of genes and the localization of their encoded products into mitochondria for anaerobic reactions to occur158. Moreover, this avenue should be approached with caution, as it could disrupt existing symbiotic relationships and ecological balances. Enhanced nitrogen acquisition by engineered fungal symbionts may modify nutrient limitation patterns, potentially favoring plant species that are more responsive to increased nitrogen availability and thereby influencing community composition and competitive dynamics. At larger spatial scales, widespread deployment of such technologies could affect nutrient cycling, soil microbial community structure, carbon sequestration dynamics, and plant–microbe coevolutionary relationships. Changes in the balance between nitrogen-limited and phosphorus-limited systems could also lead to shifts in dominant vegetation types and ecosystem functioning176,177, although the magnitude and direction of these effects remain difficult to predict. Therefore, while engineering fungi to enhance nutrient uptake holds potential, it is imperative to consider the broader ecological implications and limitations. A holistic approach that integrates molecular biology with ecological principles is essential to ensure that such interventions are both effective and sustainable within their environmental contexts.Lastly, rhizosphere engineering, which involves using plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria to enhance plant growth, has been summarized previously178. Fungi with known benefits could be applied in a similar manner to colonize or interact with plants to enhance their growth. The potential benefits of using AM fungi to enhance host plant health have also been summarized previously179. This review highlights how these fungi can be leveraged for their existing traits to reduce heavy metal toxins, defend against pathogens and pests, and improve drought tolerance in host plants.Metabolic engineering of soil fungi for enhanced bioremediation and greenhouse gas mitigationSoil-borne fungi play a pivotal role in bioremediation, utilizing their native enzymatic capabilities to degrade environmental waste and threats such as plastics, petroleum hydrocarbons, and pesticides. This degradation process not only detoxifies contaminated environments but also mitigates the release of GHGs that would otherwise result from the accumulation and breakdown of these pollutants. In this regard, isolates of the endophyte Pestalotiopsis microspora have been found to be capable of degrading polyester polyurethane and utilizing it as a carbon source180. The molecular characterization of this activity creates new possibilities for engineering metabolic properties in other soil fungi to reduce microplastics in the environment. The development of bioinformatics tools to mine for biosynthetic gene clusters in fungi could facilitate the identification of GRSP-related genes and pathways, but it is contingent upon the availability of genomic sequence data for AM species. The application of these technologies into soil-borne fungi should be considered as an additional means to boost carbon sequestration and is made feasible by the increasing availability of genetic tools in these biological systems. Yeasts—mainly Saccharomyces cerevisiae—are already being utilized for the production of biofuels, but these strains can be improved to increase carbon flux toward generating more or different desired products and to generate less waste191,192. Soil yeasts should also be considered for engineering platforms because they have the potential to grow under conditions that are not normally conducive to good laboratory performance193,194. Fatty acid production is another avenue that has been exploited in yeasts for capturing CO2195. This approach can be extended to other yeasts and filamentous fungi by introducing CO2-assimilating pathways.Along with these efforts, an autotrophic strain of Escherichia coli capable of utilizing CO2 as its sole carbon source has been developed through genetic engineering and laboratory evolution196. This technology could be applied to different species of fungi as well, though it would require the introduction of specific Calvin cycle enzymes and the rewiring of the host’s endogenous metabolic network.ConclusionThis review sheds light on the pivotal role that soil-borne fungi play in shaping global carbon dynamics, particularly in relation to atmospheric CO2 reduction. We have demonstrated how different fungal guilds, including mycorrhizal, saprotrophic, and endophytic fungi, contribute to carbon sequestration by both enhancing soil carbon storage and promoting plant health and development. We showed that the response of these fungi to global warming varies; some can adapt or even thrive, whereas others encounter challenges that may hinder their ecological functions. In addition, this review emphasizes several fungal guilds that exhibit promise for applications in synthetic biology, specifically targeting the enhancement of their native carbon-capturing abilities. Nonetheless, the advancement of genetic tools for these organisms continues to be a crucial challenge, particularly given the limited understanding of many soil-associated fungal species. Although engineered soil-borne fungi present a promising avenue for enhancing carbon sequestration, it is essential to consider the biosafety aspects of introducing genetically modified organisms into natural environments. The ecological and biological ramifications of such interventions must be cautiously assessed to ensure that these organisms contribute effectively to carbon management without disrupting native microbial communities or ecosystem functions. In this regard, strategies such as incorporating genetic safeguards (e.g., self-limiting mechanisms or biocontainment systems) should be considered, as they can help prevent unintended spread or persistence of modified organisms in the environment197,198.Our review of the existing literature identifies key knowledge gaps that should be prioritized in future research. Addressing these areas through targeted, experimentally tractable approaches will help harness soil-borne fungi as tools for carbon sequestration and CO₂ reduction, supporting the development of scalable and sustainable carbon management strategies.
                
                  Determine how environmental variability (e.g., increased temperature, altered precipitation, and soil physicochemical shifts) alters soil fungal community composition and function by quantifying changes in fungal-mediated carbon sequestration rates and soil carbon persistence using defined metrics of carbon flux and stability.
                
                
                  Assess how specific combinations of fungal guilds and other soil microbiota influence carbon retention versus loss by measuring CO₂ emissions, carbon stabilization rates, and incorporation into mineral-associated organic matter in controlled microbial consortia experiments.
                
                
                  Develop and optimize synthetic biology toolkits for understudied soil fungi to improve the carbon assimilation and storage pathways described in this review, and evaluate engineered strains by quantifying carbon assimilation efficiency, biomass production, carbon stabilization, and net carbon capture under controlled and field-relevant conditions.
                
                
                  Conduct large-scale field trials across diverse ecosystems to quantify the real-world effectiveness of fungal-mediated carbon sequestration strategies using standardized metrics such as soil organic carbon accumulation and net ecosystem CO₂ flux. To support monitoring, reporting, and verification, future field studies should report quantitative measurements of net CO₂ fluxes using standardized and independently verifiable methodologies.
                
              Collectively, these targeted future objectives will enable a more rigorous evaluation of the role of soil fungi and proposed engineered and enhanced pathways in climate change mitigation and support the development of scalable, evidence-based carbon management strategies.

items.body:
Energia

Fotovoltaico in crescita del 27%, ma la domanda di elettricità in Italia raggiunge il picco dal 2014

Roberto Torcolacci

-

23 Ottobre 2026

A settembre 2026 il fotovoltaico italiano ha segnato il suo mese migliore di sempre in termini di crescita annuale, eppure non è bastato. La domanda di elettricità nel paese ha raggiunto 27,8 TWh, il livello più alto registrato in un mese di settembre dal 2014: un dato che racconta molto di più di un semplice picco stagionale. Il quadro del fotovoltaico Italia 2026 è quello di una transizione energetica che corre, ma deve fare i conti con un fabbisogno che corre ancora più veloce.
Il solare accelera: +27% in un mese solo
I dati elaborati da Terna e riportati da Solareb2b raccontano un settembre da record per l’energia solare. La produzione fotovoltaica ha raggiunto 5,316 GWh, con un incremento del 27,1% rispetto allo stesso mese del 2025. In termini assoluti, significa circa 1,1 miliardi di chilowattora in più rispetto a un anno fa: una quantità significativa, equivalente al consumo mensile di centinaia di migliaia di abitazioni.
Il dato non è un caso isolato. Guardando all’intero periodo gennaio-settembre 2026, la crescita del fotovoltaico si attesta al +20,5% rispetto ai primi nove mesi del 2025. Una traiettoria costante, che segnala come la capacità installata stia finalmente traducendosi in produzione reale su scala rilevante.
A settembre, il solare ha coperto il 22,09% della produzione elettrica totale (su 24.065 GWh generati complessivamente) e il 19,15% della domanda. Quasi un quinto del fabbisogno nazionale soddisfatto da pannelli fotovoltaici in un singolo mese autunnale: un risultato che fino a pochi anni fa sarebbe sembrato ottimistico persino nelle proiezioni più favorevoli.Leggi ancheFotovoltaico: perovskite efficienza record, presto sul mercato?Nucleare, la Francia verso un futuro senza atomo?
Domanda ai massimi dal 2014: perché cresce il fabbisogno elettrico
Il problema è che dall’altra parte della bilancia i consumi non stanno fermi. I 27,8 TWh richiesti a settembre 2026 rappresentano un aumento del 6,5% su base mensile — pari a circa +4,6% depurato dagli effetti di calendario e dal numero di giorni lavorativi. Non si trattava di un’estate eccezionalmente calda prolungata oltre il normale: la domanda elevata riflette tendenze strutturali più profonde.
→ Leggi anche: Settore elettrico italiano richiede 200 miliardi di euro in 10 anni per la transizione energetica entro 2035: lo studio Teha-Elettricità Futura
Tra i fattori che spingono verso l’alto i consumi elettrici italiani ci sono dinamiche ormai consolidate: la diffusione delle pompe di calore in sostituzione delle caldaie a gas, la crescita del parco auto elettrico, la progressiva elettrificazione dei processi industriali, e l’espansione dei data center legati all’intelligenza artificiale e ai servizi cloud. Sono tutti settori in forte espansione, e tutti si alimentano di elettricità.
Il risultato è che anche un fotovoltaico in crescita del 27% fatica a tenere il passo con una domanda che sale in modo sostenuto. Il saldo tra produzione rinnovabile e fabbisogno rimane positivo rispetto al passato, ma il margine si assottiglia quando l’idroelettrico — altra fonte rinnovabile fondamentale per il sistema italiano — non riesce a compensare.
Il nodo idroelettrico e la dipendenza dalle importazioni
Il sistema elettrico italiano si regge storicamente su un mix che vede il fotovoltaico affiancarsi all’idroelettrico, al termoelettrico e alle importazioni dall’estero. Quando uno di questi pilastri vacilla, gli altri devono compensare. A settembre 2026, secondo le indicazioni disponibili, la produzione idroelettrica ha subito una contrazione rispetto ai livelli dell’anno precedente — un fenomeno legato alla variabilità delle precipitazioni e alla disponibilità idrica nei bacini alpini e appenninici.
Questa riduzione ha avuto un effetto diretto sul bilancio energetico nazionale: per coprire la domanda record, l’Italia ha dovuto ricorrere in misura maggiore alle importazioni di elettricità e a un utilizzo più intenso delle centrali termoelettriche. Entrambe le soluzioni hanno implicazioni ambientali ed economiche non trascurabili. Le importazioni dipendono dalla disponibilità e dai prezzi sui mercati europei, mentre il termoelettrico — basato prevalentemente su gas naturale — produce emissioni di CO₂ e resta esposto alla volatilità delle quotazioni del gas.
È qui che emerge la fragilità strutturale di un sistema in transizione: le rinnovabili crescono, ma la loro intermittenza richiede un sistema di bilanciamento robusto. Senza adeguate capacità di accumulo e senza una rete sufficientemente flessibile, i picchi di domanda continuano a essere coperti da fonti fossili.
→ Leggi anche: Settore elettrico italiano, 200 miliardi di euro di investimenti in 10 anni secondo lo studio Teha-Elettricità Futura
Fotovoltaico Italia 2026: tra record e infrastrutture da completare
Il dato del +27,1% a settembre è, oggettivamente, una buona notizia. Indica che i nuovi impianti installati stanno producendo, che la filiera funziona, che gli investimenti degli anni precedenti stanno generando risultati concreti. Il report mensile di Solareb2b basato sui dati Terna lo conferma con numeri precisi.
Ma il fotovoltaico italiano nel 2026 vive anche un paradosso: più cresce la capacità installata, più emergono i colli di bottiglia che ne limitano l’efficacia. Le connessioni alla rete di distribuzione restano un ostacolo per molti nuovi impianti, soprattutto nel Mezzogiorno, dove il potenziale solare è massimo ma le infrastrutture di rete sono più datate. L’accumulo energetico — batterie stazionarie, sistemi di storage industriale — è ancora insufficiente rispetto alla quantità di energia solare che potrebbe essere immagazzinata nelle ore centrali della giornata per essere usata la sera o nei giorni nuvolosi.
Sul fronte industriale, la crescita del fotovoltaico è trainata soprattutto dagli impianti di grande taglia — quelli su capannoni, aree produttive, terreni agricoli in configurazione agrivoltaico — mentre il segmento residenziale mostra segnali di rallentamento, in parte legato all’esaurimento degli incentivi più generosi degli anni scorsi.
Cosa dice il gap tra produzione e domanda sul futuro energetico italiano
Il settembre 2026 italiano racconta una storia che vale la pena leggere con attenzione: non è la storia di un fotovoltaico che non funziona, ma quella di un paese che sta elettrificando la propria economia più velocemente di quanto riesca ad adeguare le infrastrutture di rete e di accumulo.
Questo disallineamento ha conseguenze pratiche. Nei mesi estivi, quando il sole è abbondante e la produzione solare è massima, si registrano già ore in cui l’elettricità prodotta supera quella consumata — e parte di essa viene sprecata o ceduta all’estero a prezzi bassissimi. Nei mesi in cui la domanda sale e le condizioni meteorologiche riducono la produzione rinnovabile, il sistema torna a dipendere da fonti fossili e importazioni. Il fotovoltaico, da solo, non può risolvere questo squilibrio.
La risposta non è rallentare l’installazione di nuovi impianti solari — sarebbe controproducente — ma accelerare parallelamente su tre fronti: potenziamento della rete elettrica, espansione dei sistemi di accumulo e gestione attiva della domanda, coinvolgendo industrie e consumatori nella modulazione dei propri consumi nelle ore di maggiore disponibilità rinnovabile. Il dato di settembre 2026 è un segnale chiaro che questa fase del lavoro non può più essere rinviata.
